newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Russia, China objecting to U.N. Haiti mission.
newsitem.headline: Russia, China objecting to U.N. Haiti mission.

text.p: The Security Council, unable to agree on the future of the U.N. peacekeeping mission in Haiti, extended the force for nearly a week while members continued negotiations on Friday.

The council adopted a so-called "technical rollover" that would renew the operation of 1,300 troops and 286 civilians until Thursday after Russia insisted the military mission should be closed down altogether sometime in 1997. The current mandate expired on Friday.
Most council members have accepted a recommendation from Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali that the force should stay in Haiti until June 30, when the issue will be discussed again.
The United States and Canada, which heads the operation, do not want to be tied down at this time to a definite timetable on ending the force but may have to work out some compromise.
Russian ambassador Sergei Lavrov said: "This is the time to reduce the mission and to have the last extension."

His deputy, Yuri Fedotov, said Moscow was less concerned with the length of the extension than that it should be the last one. "We can even consider and envisage the possibiity of a slight increase in the police personnel if we agree to reduce the military component," he said.
He said the Haiti operation had little to do anymore with traditional peacekeeping.

China, which in June secured a reduction in the number of U.N. troops and police in Haiti, has advocated an extension of only five months, subject to renewal. Diplomats said this would allow Beijing to get more concessions from Haiti on its ties to Taiwan.

Beijing opposed the mission a year ago because it was angry at Haiti's ties with Taiwan, which it considers a renegade province. But relations have improved since a visit to Haiti in June by China's U.N. ambassador, Qin Huasun.

During the last renewal, in February, China threatened to veto the military force in Haiti unless its numbers were cut, prompting Canada to rescue the mission by paying for its own troops for six months.
Currently, the United Nations is paying for 600 troops, with the remaining 700 financed separately by Canada and the United States. Canada is fielding more than 700 troops and Pakistan more than 500.
President Rene Preval has asked for an eight-month renewal as a minimum.

One of the operation's main tasks is to train and monitor Haiti's fledgling police, which replaced paramilitary contingents loyal to the military junta that overthrew elected President Jean Bertrand Aristide in 1991.

Aristide was restored to power three years later by a U.S.-led multinational force. The United Nations took over peacekeeping in March 1995 with 6,000 troops, and the number has reduced steadily since then.
